hints: Look back at the stem - which exact pest does Cry1Ac kill, and what does that tell you about how narrow its action is?
Think about what happens to bees, pollinators and natural predators if an insect-killer is very specific compared with a broad-spectrum killer.
walkthrough:
Why specificity matters**
Different Cry proteins kill different insects. Cry1Ac is useful because it matches the real problem in cotton - the larvae of moths and butterflies including the cotton bollworm Helicoverpa zea. Other Cry types might not kill this pest.

Protecting helpful insects**
A specific toxin only kills the target pest and leaves useful insects alive. That means bees and other pollinators keep pollinating, and natural predators keep eating pests. The food web stays intact and biodiversity is protected, which is a clear advantage over a toxin that kills many insect types.
Final answer: Cry1Ac specifically kills / targets the cotton bollworm pest; does not kill beneficial insects such as pollinators / bees / predators of pests, so conserves biodiversity / food webs.

hints: A bare coding sequence inserted into plant DNA will just sit there - what process must happen first before any Cry protein can be made?
Recall which DNA region RNA polymerase must attach to, and how that region can control how much protein is made and where.
walkthrough:
Genes need a switch**
The coding sequence is only the instructions for the protein. For mRNA to be made, RNA polymerase must bind to DNA and start transcription. The promoter is the binding site that switches the gene on.

Controlling expression**
Without a plant promoter the bacterial gene would not be transcribed in the cotton cell. The promoter ensures the template strand is transcribed and translated, and it can control how much Cry protein is made and in which parts of the plant it is produced.
Final answer: Promoter allows the inserted gene to be expressed / transcribed; RNA polymerase binds at promoter to control quantity and location of Cry1Ac production.

hints: The marker gene and the Cry gene are put into the same genetic package - so if a cell gets one, what else has it almost certainly got?
If every cell is exposed to herbicide, think about which cells will live and which will die based on whether transformation worked.
Link survival after spraying to identification - what does a surviving plant tell you about its genes?
walkthrough:
Linked genes travel together**
The herbicide resistance gene is placed right next to the Cry1Ac gene in the vector. Transformation is inefficient, so most cells do not take up DNA. But any cell that does take up the package gets both genes together.

Use herbicide as a sieve**
Spray all the treated cells or young plants with that herbicide. Non-transformed cells have no resistance and die.

Survivors are the transformants**
Surviving cells must possess the resistance gene and therefore almost certainly also possess the Cry1Ac gene. That is how the marker identifies successful insect-resistant GM plants without having to test every plant for Bt protein directly.

Final answer: Insert herbicide resistance gene next to Bt / Cry1Ac gene; spray / apply herbicide to transformed cells / plants; only survivors contain the package so survivors identified as successful GM / insect-resistant plants.

hints: Compare the two cost rows one by one - in which row is Bt higher and in which row is Bt lower?
Add seed + insecticide for each column to see which system is more expensive overall, and quote the numbers with units.
walkthrough:
Split the costs**
Seed cost: Bt cotton $629$ rupees ha-1 is much higher than non-GM at $196$ rupees ha-1. Insecticide cost shows the opposite: Bt cotton $503$ rupees ha-1 is lower than non-GM at $851$ rupees ha-1, because the plant makes its own insecticide.

Overall comparison**
Add them: Bt total = $629 + 503 = 1132$ rupees ha-1. Non-GM total = $196 + 851 = 1047$ rupees ha-1. So Bt saves on spray but costs more overall to grow because the expensive seed outweighs the insecticide saving.
Final answer: Bt seed cost higher ($629$ vs $196$ rupees ha-1) but Bt insecticide cost lower ($503$ vs $851$ rupees ha-1); total cost higher for Bt ($1132$ vs $1047$ rupees ha-1).

hints: Net income is higher for Bt, but what must a poor farmer pay at the start of the season before any harvest is sold?
walkthrough:
Cash at planting time**
Table 4.1 shows Bt seed costs over three times as much as non-GM seed. Even though Bt gives higher net income later, many small farmers cannot afford the high upfront cost, so they choose cheap non-GM seed that is affordable overall.
Final answer: Non-GM seeds are cheaper / more affordable to buy / cheaper overall to grow.

hints: The question bans gene technology, so think of the traditional breeding method farmers have used for centuries to combine traits.
What two parents would you cross if you want offspring that are both insect-resistant and able to grow in drought?
One cross is not enough to get a true-breeding variety - what must you do with the best offspring generation after generation?
walkthrough:
Choose the breeding route**
Without gene technology the method is selective breeding, also called artificial selection. You start with existing variation: Bt cotton that has insect resistance but poor drought growth, and another cotton variety that already grows well in dry conditions.

Make the cross and select**
Cross-pollinate Bt cotton with the drought-adapted variety. Among the offspring, choose those plants that both produce Cry1Ac and grow well in dry conditions.

Fix the combination**
Cross those selected plants together or back to parents and keep selecting the best offspring each generation. After several generations of repeated selection, you obtain a true-breeding variety that combines Bt insect resistance with drought adaptation.

Final answer: Use selective breeding / artificial selection; cross Bt cotton with a variety that grows well in dry / drought conditions; select offspring with Bt trait and drought tolerance and repeat crossing / selection for several generations.
